captions.instagram:
How does a lock work?

Slide a key into a lock cut in half and watch five tiny pin stacks rise to one line. Cut your own key, count the million possible codes, throw a deadbolt, and see what levers, dials and chips do instead.

→ A door lock is a plug that wants to turn and five stacks of pins that stop it.
→ The right key lifts every pin stack to the shear line, and the plug is free to turn.
→ Get one cut wrong by half a millimetre and a pin stays across the gap. The plug is stuck.
→ Six depths on five pins is 7,776 keys. Six pins and ten depths make a million.
→ A master-keyed lock has an extra thin pin in some stacks, so two different keys line up.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/lockclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a lock work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Slide a key into a lock cut in half and watch five tiny pin stacks rise to one line. Cut your own key, count the million possible codes, throw a deadbolt, and see what levers, dials and chips do instead.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/lockclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/lockclear

In this video:
• A plug that is pinned in place. Most door locks are pin-tumbler cylinders.
• The right key lines up every stack. Each cut in the key holds one stack at a set height.
• A code with thousands of answers. The depths of the cuts are a code.
• The bolt does the holding. The cylinder only decides who may turn it.
• Levers, wards and wafers. A lever lock, the kind in a steel almirah, lifts flat levers until a slot in each lines up for a peg on the bolt.
• No key at all. A combination dial parks three notched wheels one at a time until a bar can drop into all three notches.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
